children: Millions of Americans use mail-order pharmacies from Canada and other countries to personally import medication for a fraction of the U.S. cost. That could soon end with a new rule going into effect on Oct. 22.
Under the rule, prescription medication mailed from abroad must go through a customs process requiring a licensed customs broker and a financial guarantee.
The rule is part of the broader suspension of the duty-free de minimis exemption for imports valued at $800 or less last year.

While personal importation of medication is technically barred under FDA rules, customs agents historically waved through such packages rather than individually checking each one against the agency's criteria.
The U.S. government previously said the new rule aimed to crack down on illegal contraband that enters the country through low-value foreign shipments.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told
that the FDA would continue to evaluate personal imports on a case-by-case basis.

According to the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation, consumers can save an average of 65% by buying prescription medication from licensed Canadian pharmacies. Over 4M Americans rely on personal drug importation.
"These are cash-strapped, uninsured or underinsured people; many senior citizens on fixed incomes," Tim Smith, general manager of the Canadian International Pharmacy Association, told

About four in ten U.S. adults don't take their medication as prescribed due to high prices, a KFF poll found earlier this year. Many of them take over-the-counter drugs instead or don't fill their prescriptions, while others cut pills in half or skip doses.

title: Personal imports of cheaper prescription drugs will soon get trickier
